checks.claim: Key: once the thermometer stops climbing, the weight and the water share one temperature (thermal equilibrium)
checks.note: Grokipedia: heat flows from A to B 'until both reach the same final temperature, at which point equilibrium is established'.

checks.claim: Wrong: the weight is as cool as the water was at first (final temperature lies between the two starting temperatures)
checks.note: OpenStax Example 14.3: 150 C aluminium pan and 20 C water end at 59.1 C; heat lost by the pan equals heat gained by the water. Grokipedia's Tf formula is a weighted average, so it lies between.

checks.claim: Wrong: the water is as hot as the boiling water was
checks.note: The cup ends below the weight's starting temperature, same reasoning.

checks.claim: Wrong: the weight has no heat left in it at all
checks.note: Flow stops at a shared temperature well above absolute zero; the weight keeps its thermal energy.

checks.claim: Context: heat flows hot to cool until the same temperature, somewhere between where each began, then stops; the weight is still warm
Key: heat passes from the ankle into the ice pack
checks.note: NSTA: 'Thermal energy can move only from a warmer object or area to a cooler object or area, never the other way around'; best answer 'The heat from the lemonade moved into the ice'.

checks.claim: Wrong: cold flows from the ice pack into the ankle; cold in and heat out
checks.note: NSTA calls talk of 'cold' moving a misnomer for thermal energy moving warmer to cooler; cold is not a substance that flows.

checks.claim: Wrong: heat from the ice pack into the ankle
checks.note: Heat flows spontaneously only from the warmer body (ankle) to the cooler one (ice).

checks.claim: Context: heat leaves the ankle and melts the ice; the ankle feels cold because it is losing heat
Key: conduction, particles bump their neighbours passing energy on, while the metal stays put
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'successive collisions or vibrations of particles, such as electrons, atoms, or phonons', 'without any net displacement or bulk motion of the material'; in metals delocalized electrons carry most of it (still 'particles'). OpenStax 14.5: collisions pass energy from the faster molecule to the slower.

checks.claim: Wrong: an invisible heat fluid seeps up (caloric)
checks.note: Caloric was the abandoned 18th-century theory; the context presents it as a historical idea given up, not as true.

checks.claim: Wrong: the hottest metal creeps up toward the top
checks.note: No bulk motion of the material in conduction.

checks.claim: Wrong: rays of heat shine up inside the metal
checks.note: That describes radiation; heat through a solid by contact is conduction ('heat transfer through stationary matter by physical contact').

checks.claim: Context: many scientists of the late 1700s called heat an invisible fluid, caloric; experiments showed heat is energy; given up in the 1800s
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'invisible, imponderable fluid'; Lavoisier and Laplace formalised it in the 1780s, name coined 1785-1787; Rumford 1798 and Joule 1840s undermined it; superseded by Helmholtz, Clausius, Kelvin, fully supplanted by the 1860s.

checks.claim: Key: purple rises up the heated side, crosses the top, falls down the far side
checks.note: schoolphysics: crystals fall close to one side, heat the base under them, colour will 'rise up this side, go across the top and then fall down the other side of the beaker'.

checks.claim: Wrong: up the far side, down the heated side (reversed loop)
checks.note: Warm water rises over the heat, so the loop runs the other way.

checks.claim: Wrong: straight up then stays at the top; out evenly in every direction
checks.note: With heating continued the cooled water sinks and a loop forms (convective loop); even spreading would be diffusion alone, not what the heated beaker shows.

checks.claim: Context: warmed water grows less dense and rises, cools and sinks; a convection current carries the heat
checks.note: OpenStax: hot water 'expands, decreases in density, and rises'; convection is 'heat transfer by the macroscopic movement of a fluid'.

checks.claim: Key: a hot-water radiator warms a room mostly by convection
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'In typical heating radiators, convection accounts for approximately 70-80% of the total heat output, while radiation contributes the remaining 20-30%.' Wikipedia: such devices 'tend to transfer heat mainly by convection and might logically be called convectors'.

checks.claim: Context: a radiator gives off only about a quarter of its heat as radiation
checks.note: A quarter sits inside Grokipedia's typical 20-30%. The share does vary with design and water temperature: Siegenthaler (Plumbing & Mechanical) gives a finless single panel at low water temperature almost 60% radiant, and finned panels far less. True for a typical radiator; optional softening: 'only about a quarter of its heat, in a typical one, as radiation'.

checks.claim: Wrong: hot-water bottle on cold feet is conduction; sun-baked wall under a hand is conduction
checks.note: OpenStax: 'Conduction is heat transfer through stationary matter by physical contact.' Both are contact cases.

checks.claim: Wrong: sunlight warming car seats through the windows is radiation
checks.note: OpenStax: Earth gets almost all its energy as radiation from the Sun; sunlight passes the glass and is absorbed by the seats.

checks.claim: Key: most of a campfire's heat reaches the campers as rays (thermal radiation)
checks.note: Baird (West Texas A&M): 'almost a hundred percent of the heat that you receive from the fire is transferred through thermal radiation'. OpenStax: 'Most of the heat transfer from this fire to the observers is through infrared radiation.'

checks.claim: Wrong: warm air flowing straight out; heat that rises then spreads down
checks.note: Baird: convection 'shoots straight up into the sky and never reaches you'.

checks.claim: Wrong: through the air particle to particle (conduction)
checks.note: Baird: 'air is a poor thermal conductor'; conduction is negligible unless you touch the fire.

checks.claim: Context: thermal radiation, mostly infrared, travelling in straight lines in every direction
checks.note: Baird: 'mostly infrared waves and visible light'. Britannica: emitted in all directions without a medium; it follows the rules of light, straight lines in a uniform medium.

checks.claim: Key: Sun to slide by radiation, slide to boy by conduction
checks.note: OpenStax: warming of Earth by the Sun is 'an obvious example' of radiation; conduction is heat transfer 'by physical contact'.

checks.claim: Wrong: conduction then radiation; convection then conduction; radiation then convection
checks.note: Sunlight crosses largely empty space where neither conduction nor convection can work; the boy touches the metal, so the second step is contact, not a moving fluid.

checks.claim: Context: convection needs a moving liquid or gas
checks.note: OpenStax: 'Convection is the heat transfer by the macroscopic movement of a fluid.'

checks.claim: Key: fibreglass traps air in pockets too small for it to flow
checks.note: OpenStax: fur, fibre and fibreglass trap air in 'spaces too small to support convection'; air 'is a poor conductor and thus a good insulator'. Grokipedia Glass wool: 'small, stationary air voids'.

checks.claim: Stem: solid glass lets heat through quickly compared with the mats
checks.note: OpenStax table 14.3: glass 0.84, glass wool 0.042, air 0.023 J/s m C, so solid glass conducts about 20 times better than glass wool.

checks.claim: Wrong: threads soak up heat and store it
checks.note: Glass wool works by low conductivity of trapped still air, not by storing heat.

checks.claim: Wrong: threads are hollow with a vacuum inside
checks.note: Ordinary rotary-spun insulation glass fibres are 'primarily solid'; hollow fibres exist only in patents and hold gas, not vacuum. Grokipedia credits trapped air.

checks.claim: Wrong: thin glass threads cannot carry heat
checks.note: Glass conducts (0.84); the context rightly says the threads still conduct a little.

checks.claim: Stem: James Dewar made the FIRST vacuum flask, at the Royal Institution in London, in 1892
checks.note: Grokipedia and Wikipedia credit Dewar with inventing the vacuum flask in 1892 at the RI, and the RI calls it 'Dewar's first-ever vacuum flask' (his first, not the world's). But earlier vacuum vessels are documented: the RI says Dewar himself made a vacuum-insulated goblet with Peter Tait in 1872 (https://rigb.org/node/3131); TU Chemnitz says Adolf Weinhold described a double-walled glass bottle with the air pumped out of the gap, holding low temperatures for hours, in his 1881 'Physikalische Demonstrationen', and that Dewar used a double-walled metal vessel in 1874. 'The first' is a priority claim the question does not need. Fix: 'James Dewar, a Scottish chemist, built his vacuum flask at the Royal Institution in London in 1892.' (or 'invented the vacuum flask', the encyclopaedias' wording).

checks.claim: Dewar was a Scottish chemist; Royal Institution, London; 1892
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'Scottish chemist and physicist', Fullerian Professor of Chemistry at the RI from 1877. RI: created in 1892, first shown at the RI on Christmas Day 1892.

checks.claim: Key: built to hold gases chilled until they turned to liquid
checks.note: RI: 'Created in 1892 to hold liquefied gases at extremely low temperatures.' Grokipedia: liquid air and oxygen, later liquid hydrogen (1898).

checks.claim: Wrong: molten metals; germs kept at body heat; ice on sea voyages
checks.note: None was its purpose; it was built for cryogenic research.

checks.claim: Stem: double glass walls with a vacuum between them slow heat in or out
checks.note: Double-walled glass vessel, gap evacuated.

checks.claim: Context: liquefying gases by extreme cooling was costly, so he needed them to stay liquid long enough to study
checks.note: RI: 'Forcing gases to the extremely low temperatures at which they become liquid was a very expensive process.'

checks.claim: Context: the flask keeps cold things cold as well as hot things hot
checks.note: Grokipedia: works for chilled contents as well as hot.

checks.claim: Context: a company called Thermos began making it for everyday use in 1904
checks.note: Wikipedia: 'Dewar's design was quickly transformed into a commercial item in 1904'; Burger and Aschenbrenner named it Thermos. Grokipedia: Thermos GmbH, Berlin, commercialised it in 1904. RI: 'patented and renamed for industrial use in 1904 by the Thermos company'.

checks.claim: Key: a near-vacuum gap blocks conduction and convection
checks.note: Wikipedia: the partly evacuated gap cuts heat transfer by conduction and convection. Grokipedia: the vacuum removes the gas that would carry heat by conduction and convection.

checks.claim: Wrong: any choice naming radiation as blocked by the vacuum
checks.note: OpenStax: 'no medium is required for electromagnetic waves to propagate'; radiation crosses a vacuum, so the three choices with radiation are wrong.

checks.claim: Context: conduction needs particles to collide, convection needs a fluid to flow
Context: sunlight crosses empty space to Earth as radiation
checks.note: OpenStax: space between Earth and Sun 'largely empty'; Earth gets almost all its energy as radiation from the Sun.

checks.claim: Context: the walls facing the gap are silvered to reflect radiation back
checks.note: Wikipedia: 'Heat transfer by thermal radiation may be minimized by silvering flask surfaces facing the gap.'

checks.claim: Key: the aluminium coating reflects the body's radiated heat back toward him
checks.note: Grokipedia: reflects 'up to 97% of radiant body heat back toward the user'.

checks.claim: Stem: thin plastic sheet coated with a very thin layer of aluminium; given to marathon runners at the finish
checks.note: PET film with vacuum-deposited aluminium; race organisers often give them to marathoners after races.

checks.claim: Wrong: soaks up and stores heat rays; draws warmth from the air; gives off heat of its own
checks.note: Shiny metal reflects most incident radiation and absorbs little (OpenStax: silver object a poor absorber); the blanket has no heat source and cannot pump heat from cooler air.

checks.claim: Context: reflects up to 97 percent of radiated infrared heat
checks.note: Wikipedia: 'reflects up to 97% of radiated heat'. Grokipedia also gives 'up to 90%' in its introduction, but says the figure is for radiant heat only; 'up to 97 percent' of radiated heat is supported.

checks.claim: Context: the sheet blocks wind and holds in moisture, cutting convection and evaporation
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'barrier to wind and air movement'; the film 'limits evaporative heat loss'.

unit_notes: 10 ok, 1 uncertain. b91129d092: 'made the first vacuum flask' is a priority claim with documented earlier vacuum vessels (Dewar's own 1872 goblet with Tait, Weinhold 1881 per TU Chemnitz); drop 'the first'. 7be41b0d20: the radiator's radiant share ('about a quarter') matches Grokipedia's typical 20-30% but varies with design (a finless panel at low water temperature can be near 60% radiant, per Plumbing & Mechanical); the key stands, optional softening of the context to 'in a typical one'.
